lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • Hazardous effects of shopping bags are studied in Environmental Chemistry.
  • Polystyrene is a man-made polymer; starch, protein and cellulose are natural polymers.
  • Sulphur forms crystals of rhombic shape.
  • Milk is a colloidal solution (a colloid).
  • Concrete mixture is a heterogeneous mixture.
  • A suspension is a mixture in which tiny visible particles of a substance are dispersed through a medium.
  • A solution of KClO₃ has a solubility of about 13.2 g per 100 cm³ at 40 C; decreasing the temperature decreases its solubility.
  • The rate of hydrolysis of starch under different conditions of temperature is studied in Physical Chemistry.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
First, chemistry covers a very wide and complex subject, so no one person can study all of it in depth. Second, dividing it lets scientists concentrate on one specific area and make faster progress in it. Third, each branch develops its own methods and instruments suited to its own problems, which leads to new discoveries and applications.

Reactions involving electrons outside the nucleus are ordinary chemical reactions, studied by the main branches of chemistry such as Physical, Inorganic and Organic Chemistry. Reactions taking place inside the nucleus are studied by Nuclear Chemistry, which deals with radioactivity and changes in the nuclei of atoms.

Analytical chemistry solves problems of separation, identification and measurement: what substances are present in a sample, and in what amount or concentration. It uses modern instruments to analyse materials such as water, food, medicines, minerals and industrial products.

Graphite is made of many hexagonal layers of carbon atoms stacked on top of one another. Graphene is a single one-atom-thick hexagonal layer of carbon atoms. In short, graphene is one layer, while graphite is a stack of many such layers.

Graphene is the thinnest and one of the strongest materials known, yet it is light and flexible. It conducts electricity and heat better than most materials and is almost transparent. Because of this it is used in electronics, batteries, sensors, strong composite materials and medical devices.

Most material things belong to mixtures. Very few things in daily life are pure elements or pure compounds. Air, water from natural sources, soil, rocks, food, milk and alloys are all mixtures of two or more substances mixed in any ratio.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Diamond is brilliant because it has a very high refractive index (2.42) and it bends light strongly, so light entering the stone is totally internally reflected many times and then dispersed into colours before it leaves. Yes, its brilliance can be improved by cutting it into the right shape, such as the brilliant cut, with well-placed facets, and by polishing its surfaces perfectly so that the maximum light is reflected back to the eye.

Solubility depends on how strongly the particles of the solute attract one another compared with how strongly they attract water molecules. Compounds whose particles are held together very strongly, or which attract water only weakly, dissolve little. Compounds that form strong attractions with water dissolve more. Temperature, pressure and the nature of both solute and solvent also affect the result.

Crystallisation by cooling works only when solubility falls sharply as temperature falls. The solubility of KNO₃ rises steeply with temperature, so cooling a hot saturated solution deposits a large crop of crystals. The solubility of NaCl changes very little with temperature, so cooling deposits almost no crystals. Salt is therefore recovered by evaporating the water, not by cooling.

Graphite is slippery because it is built of flat layers of carbon atoms, and the layers are held together only by weak forces. The layers slide easily over one another when touched or rubbed. This same property, the easy sliding of its layers, together with its soft and greasy feel, makes graphite a good dry lubricant.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
(a) Rate of a reaction: Physical Chemistry, which studies reaction rates.
(b) Digestion of food in human body: Biochemistry, which studies chemical processes in living organisms.
(c) Properties of colloidal solution: Physical Chemistry, which studies the behaviour of matter at molecular level.
(d) Ecosystem: Environmental Chemistry, which studies chemical phenomena in air, soil and water.
(e) Reactions taking place during fireworks: Physical Chemistry, which studies the energy and rates of rapid reactions.
(f) Measurement of absorption of wavelength with ultraviolet spectrometer: Analytical Chemistry, which uses instruments to analyse substances.

Allotropic forms are different physical forms of the same element in the same state, with different arrangements of atoms and different properties. Carbon exists as diamond, in which each carbon atom is bonded to four others in a hard three-dimensional network; as graphite, in layers of hexagonal rings; and as fullerene, in closed cage-like molecules. Sulphur exists as rhombic sulphur, stable below 96 C, and monoclinic sulphur, stable above 96 C, both made of S₈ rings but packed differently. Coal differs from diamond because coal is impure, soft, black and amorphous carbon mixed with other substances, while diamond is pure, hard, transparent, crystalline carbon.

Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute, in grams, that dissolves in 100 g (or 100 cm³) of a solvent at a given temperature to form a saturated solution. For most solid solutes, solubility increases with temperature, for example copper sulphate, sodium nitrate and potassium nitrate dissolve more in hot water. A few solids behave oppositely, for example the solubility of calcium hydroxide decreases as temperature increases. For gases, solubility in water decreases as temperature increases.

Inorganic chemistry studies elements and compounds that contain little or no carbon: metals, non-metals, salts, acids, bases and minerals, their synthesis, composition, properties and structure. Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, hydrocarbons and their derivatives, their structure, formation, properties, composition and reactions. Organic compounds are found in all forms of life and are essential for it, while inorganic compounds include fertilisers, medicines, catalysts, pigments and coatings.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • The third shell of an atom can accommodate at most 18 electrons.
  • Discharge tube experiments led to the discovery of electrons and protons.
  • Particles present in the nucleus are held together by the strong nuclear force.
  • Electrons keep themselves away from the oppositely charged nucleus by revolving around the nucleus.

lessons.title: In-chapter Exercise (book p. 17)
lessons.notes_html: By their relative atomic masses. Magnesium has a relative atomic mass of about 24 and chlorine of about 35.5, so one atom of chlorine is about one and a half times heavier than one atom of magnesium. For equal numbers of atoms, a sample of chlorine is heavier than a sample of magnesium in the ratio 35.5 to 24.

mcqs.q: By what are the atoms of magnesium and chlorine compared for heaviness in this exercise?
options: By the sizes of their nuclei only
By the colours of their compounds
mcqs.why: The notes say the atoms are compared by their relative atomic masses: magnesium about 24 and chlorine about 35.5.

mcqs.q: What is the relative atomic mass of magnesium, as given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give the relative atomic mass of magnesium as about 24, while chlorine is about 35.5.

mcqs.q: What is the relative atomic mass of chlorine, as given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give the relative atomic mass of chlorine as about 35.5, while magnesium is about 24.

mcqs.q: One atom of chlorine is about how many times heavier than one atom of magnesium?
mcqs.why: Working: 35.5 / 24 = 1.479, which is about 1.5. So one chlorine atom is about one and a half times heavier than one magnesium atom, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: For equal numbers of atoms, a sample of chlorine is heavier than a sample of magnesium in which ratio?
mcqs.why: The notes say that for equal numbers of atoms, a sample of chlorine is heavier than a sample of magnesium in the ratio 35.5 to 24, from their relative atomic masses.

mcqs.q: If equal numbers of magnesium and chlorine atoms are taken, which sample is heavier?
options: Both samples have exactly equal mass
mcqs.why: Chlorine's relative atomic mass (35.5) is greater than magnesium's (24), so for equal numbers of atoms the chlorine sample is heavier, in the ratio 35.5 to 24.

mcqs.q: By how much does the relative atomic mass of chlorine exceed that of magnesium?
mcqs.why: Working: 35.5 - 24 = 11.5. So chlorine's relative atomic mass exceeds magnesium's by 11.5 units.

mcqs.q: Ten atoms of each element are compared. What are their total relative masses?
mcqs.why: Working: 10 x 24 = 240 for magnesium, and 10 x 35.5 = 355 for chlorine. Equal numbers keep the same heaviness ratio, so chlorine totals 355 against magnesium's 240.

mcqs.q: By about what percentage is one chlorine atom heavier than one magnesium atom?
mcqs.why: Working: difference = 35.5 - 24 = 11.5; percentage = 11.5 / 24 x 100 = 47.9 percent. So a chlorine atom is about 47.9 percent heavier than a magnesium atom.

mcqs.q: What is the ratio of the relative atomic mass of magnesium to that of chlorine?
mcqs.why: Magnesium's relative atomic mass is about 24 and chlorine's is about 35.5, so the ratio of magnesium to chlorine is 24 to 35.5.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
The nucleus contains the protons and neutrons, which are about 1836 times heavier than an electron. The electrons outside the nucleus have almost no mass compared with them. Therefore, although the nucleus is tiny in size, it holds practically the whole mass of the atom.

Elements are different because they have different numbers of protons, that is, different atomic numbers. The number of protons fixes the number of electrons in a neutral atom, and the electronic arrangement fixes the chemical properties. Hence each element behaves differently from every other element.

Mass number = 210, atomic number = 83. Number of neutrons = mass number minus atomic number = 210 minus 83 = 127. So 127 neutrons are present in this atom of bismuth.

An atom absorbs energy when one of its electrons jumps from a lower energy shell to a higher energy shell. An atom evolves energy when an excited electron falls back from a higher shell to a lower shell, and the energy is given out, usually as light of a definite wavelength.

mcqs.q: Why does the tiny nucleus hold practically the whole mass of the atom?
options: Because the electrons are heavier than the nucleus
Because it contains the protons and neutrons, which are much heavier than an electron, while the electrons have almost no mass in comparison
Because the nucleus is the largest part of the atom
Because the electrons are inside the nucleus
mcqs.why: The notes say the nucleus contains the protons and neutrons, which are about 1836 times heavier than an electron, so although tiny, it holds practically the whole mass of the atom.

mcqs.q: Protons and neutrons are about how many times heavier than an electron?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the protons and neutrons in the nucleus are about 1836 times heavier than an electron.

mcqs.q: Why is each element different from every other element?
options: Because elements have different numbers of protons, that is, different atomic numbers
Because elements have different colours only
Because elements have different numbers of neutrons only
Because elements have different masses of electrons only
mcqs.why: The notes say elements are different because they have different numbers of protons, that is, different atomic numbers, which fix their electronic arrangement and chemical properties.

mcqs.q: What does the number of protons in an atom fix?
options: Only the size of the nucleus
Only the number of neutrons present
Only the mass of each electron
The number of electrons in a neutral atom, and through the electronic arrangement, the chemical properties
mcqs.why: The notes say the number of protons fixes the number of electrons in a neutral atom, and the electronic arrangement fixes the chemical properties of the element.

mcqs.q: An atom has mass number 210 and atomic number 83. How many neutrons does it contain?
mcqs.why: Working: number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 210 - 83 = 127. So 127 neutrons are present in this atom of bismuth.

mcqs.q: In the bismuth example (mass number 210, atomic number 83), how many protons does the atom contain?
mcqs.why: The atomic number is the number of protons, and the notes give the atomic number as 83, so the atom contains 83 protons; the remaining 210 - 83 = 127 are neutrons.

mcqs.q: When does an atom absorb energy?

When an excited electron falls back to a lower shell
When one of its electrons jumps from a lower energy shell to a higher energy shell
When a proton leaves the nucleus
mcqs.why: The notes say an atom absorbs energy when one of its electrons jumps from a lower energy shell to a higher energy shell.

mcqs.q: When does an atom evolve (give out) energy?
options: When an electron jumps from a lower shell to a higher shell
When an electron is absorbed into the nucleus
When the atom gains a new proton
When an excited electron falls back from a higher shell to a lower shell
mcqs.why: The notes say an atom evolves energy when an excited electron falls back from a higher shell to a lower shell, and the energy is given out.

mcqs.q: In what form is the energy usually given out when an excited electron falls back to a lower shell?
options: As light of a definite wavelength
As a new neutron in the nucleus
As a chemical bond with another atom

lessons.notes_html:
The first shell lies closest to the nucleus, so its electrons are held most strongly and have the lowest energy. The second shell is farther from the nucleus, so its electrons are held less strongly and possess higher energy. Energy of the shells therefore increases as we move away from the nucleus.

At normal pressure the gas molecules are crowded, and the electrons knocked out of them collide with molecules again and again, so no steady stream reaches the other end. When the pressure is lowered, the molecules become few and far apart, so the electrons travel freely across the tube and the cathode rays can be observed.

The cathode rays were found to have the same charge-to-mass ratio no matter which gas was used in the tube and no matter which metal the electrodes were made of. Similarly, the positively charged canal rays showed the same kind of particles from different gases. Since the particles did not depend on the material used, scientists concluded that electrons, and likewise protons, are the same in all elements.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
The electron was discovered through discharge tube experiments. When a high voltage was applied across a gas at low pressure, rays travelled from the cathode to the anode. These cathode rays were bent by electric and magnetic fields, showing they were negatively charged particles, and Thomson measured their charge-to-mass ratio and named them electrons. The proton was discovered through canal rays: Goldstein found positively charged rays travelling in the opposite direction through holes in the cathode. Rutherford later showed that the lightest of these positive particles, from hydrogen, is a fundamental particle of all nuclei, and it was named the proton.

A hydrogen atom is the simplest atom. Its nucleus contains a single proton and no neutron. A single electron revolves around this nucleus in the first shell. Its atomic number is 1 and its mass number is 1, and its electronic configuration is 1.

Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, and it fixes the identity of the element. Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Relative atomic mass is the average mass of the atoms of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; it is expressed in atomic mass units (amu), where 1 amu equals one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Metals lose their outer electrons easily because they have low ionisation energies and their nuclei hold the outer electrons weakly; they are electropositive. Non-metals gain electrons easily because they have high electron affinities and nearly complete outer shells; they are electronegative.

In small covalent molecules the forces between the molecules are very weak. Only a small amount of heat energy is needed to overcome these weak intermolecular forces and separate the molecules. They therefore boil at low temperatures and exist as gases or low boiling liquids at room temperature.

Diamond is such an element. It is a crystalline solid in which every carbon atom is joined to four other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds in a three-dimensional network, which is why diamond is extremely hard.

The metallic bond makes metals malleable and ductile. The positive metal ions sit in a sea of mobile electrons, and when a force is applied, one layer of ions slips over another without breaking the bond, because the mobile electrons at once hold the new positions together. Metals can therefore be beaten into sheets and drawn into wires.

Yes. Once a coordinate covalent bond is formed, it is just as strong as an ordinary covalent bond, because in both cases the two atoms are held together by a shared pair of electrons. The only difference is the origin of the pair: in a coordinate bond both electrons are donated by one atom, as in the ammonium ion and the hydroxonium ion.

In nitric acid the hydrogen atom is joined by a single bond to an oxygen atom, and that oxygen is joined by a single bond to the nitrogen atom. The nitrogen atom is joined by a double bond to a second oxygen atom and by a coordinate bond to a third oxygen atom. In the dot and cross picture the shared pairs are shown as dots for one atom and crosses for the other; the nitrogen carries a positive charge and the singly bonded oxygen carries a negative charge, so the molecule as a whole is neutral.

Hydrogen fluoride molecules are held together by strong hydrogen bonds, because fluorine is very small and highly electronegative and attracts the hydrogen of a neighbouring molecule strongly. Hydrogen chloride molecules are held only by weak dipole forces, so HCl boils at a much lower temperature and is a gas.

Water is a polar solvent, and it dissolves substances best when it can attract their particles strongly. Most covalent compounds are non-polar, so water molecules attract them only weakly, and this weak attraction cannot overcome the forces holding the covalent substance together. Polar covalent compounds such as hydrogen chloride and ammonia are exceptions and do dissolve in water.

Iodine molecules are much larger and contain many more electrons than chlorine molecules, so the London dispersion forces between iodine molecules are far stronger. Much more heat energy is needed to separate iodine molecules, so iodine is a solid at room temperature, while chlorine, with weak forces between its small molecules, is a gas.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
An ionic bond is formed by the complete transfer of one or more electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom. For example, a sodium atom gives its outer electron to a chlorine atom; both ions then have the electronic configuration of a noble gas, and the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive sodium ion and the negative chloride ion is the ionic bond. A covalent bond is formed by the mutual sharing of electron pairs between two non-metal atoms, so that both atoms complete their outer shells, for example two hydrogen atoms share one pair to form H₂, and carbon shares four pairs with four hydrogen atoms to form methane.

In a sodium chloride crystal the sodium ions and chloride ions arrange themselves in a regular three-dimensional pattern called a face-centred cubic lattice. Each sodium ion is surrounded by six chloride ions, and each chloride ion is surrounded by six sodium ions. This regular packing goes on in all directions, giving a hard, cubical crystal with a high melting point.

In a metallic bond the metal atoms release their outer electrons, which move freely through the whole piece of metal as a sea of electrons holding the positive ions together. The free electrons make metals good conductors of heat and electricity and give them their shine, because they reflect light. When a force is applied, layers of ions slip over one another without breaking the bond, so metals are malleable and ductile. The strong attraction between the ions and the electron sea gives metals high melting and boiling points, and the close packing of the ions makes them hard and heavy.

Ionic compounds are usually hard crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points, because strong electrostatic forces hold their ions together. They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not as solids, and they are usually soluble in water. Covalent compounds are usually gases, liquids or soft solids with low melting and boiling points, because only weak forces hold their molecules together. They do not conduct electricity in any state, and they are usually soluble in organic solvents rather than in water.

In graphite each carbon atom is bonded to only three other carbon atoms, so each atom has one electron left over that is not used in bonding. These extra electrons are delocalised, that is, they are free to move along the flat layers of carbon atoms. When a voltage is applied, these mobile electrons flow through the layers, so graphite conducts electricity, unlike diamond, in which all four electrons of every carbon atom are locked in bonds.

Metals are hard because the strong metallic bond holds their positive ions firmly in a regular lattice, and a large force is needed to disturb this arrangement. Metals are heavy because their atoms are closely packed together in the lattice and most metal atoms have fairly large masses, so a small volume of metal contains a large mass, giving a high density.

mcqs.why: In graphite each carbon atom is bonded to only three others, leaving one electron per atom delocalised and free to move along the layers, so graphite conducts electricity.

mcqs.q: Why are metals heavy, according to the notes?
options: Their atoms are loosely packed with large empty spaces
Their atoms are closely packed and most metal atoms have fairly large masses, giving a high density
They contain more electrons than protons in every atom
They absorb water into their lattice
mcqs.why: Metals are heavy because their atoms are closely packed together in the lattice and most metal atoms have fairly large masses, so a small volume contains a large mass.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • One gram of H₂O contains 1.002 × 10²³ atoms (the printed option misses the decimal point; the working is given in the Worked Notes lesson).
  • The correct formula of calcium phosphide is Ca₃P₂.
  • There are 6.022 × 10²³ amu (atomic mass units) in one gram.
  • The empirical formula of 2-hexene, CH₃-CH=CH-(CH₂)₂-CH₃, is CH₂.
  • 25 g of H₂SO₄ contains 0.255 moles.
  • A necklace with 6 g of diamonds contains 3.01 × 10²³ carbon atoms.
  • The mass of Al in 204 g of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, is 108 g.

mcqs.q: How many atoms are there in one gram of H2O?
mcqs.why: Working: moles of H2O = 1 / 18 = 0.0556 mol; molecules = 0.0556 x 6.022 x 10^23 = 0.334 x 10^23; each molecule has 3 atoms, so atoms = 3 x 0.334 x 10^23 = 1.002 x 10^23 atoms.

mcqs.q: What is the correct formula of calcium phosphide?
mcqs.why: The Key Facts state that the correct formula of calcium phosphide is Ca3P2, with three calcium ions balancing the charges of two phosphide ions.

mcqs.q: How many atomic mass units (amu) are there in one gram?
mcqs.why: The Key Facts state that there are 6.022 x 10^23 amu (atomic mass units) in one gram, the same value as Avogadro number of units.

mcqs.q: What is the empirical formula of 2-hexene, CH3-CH=CH-(CH2)2-CH3?
mcqs.why: 2-hexene is C6H12; dividing the subscripts 6 and 12 by their common factor 6 gives the simplest whole-number ratio 1:2, so the empirical formula stated in the notes is CH2.

mcqs.q: How many moles are there in 25 g of H2SO4?
mcqs.why: Working: molar mass of H2SO4 = 98 g/mol; moles = mass / molar mass = 25 / 98 = 0.255 mol, as stated in the Key Facts.

mcqs.q: A necklace with 6 g of diamonds contains how many carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: Working: moles of carbon = 6 / 12 = 0.5 mol; atoms = 0.5 x 6.022 x 10^23 = 3.01 x 10^23 carbon atoms, as stated in the Key Facts.

mcqs.q: What is the mass of aluminium in 204 g of aluminium oxide, Al2O3?
mcqs.why: Working: molar mass of Al2O3 = 102 g/mol; moles = 204 / 102 = 2 mol; each mole contains 2 mol of Al, so Al = 4 mol; mass = 4 x 27 = 108 g.

mcqs.q: Which compound has the highest percentage of nitrogen by mass among those compared in the book?
mcqs.why: Working: N2H4 = 28 / 32 x 100 = 87.5 percent nitrogen, higher than NH3 at 82.4 percent, urea at 46.7 percent and NH2OH at 42.4 percent.

mcqs.q: When one mole of each compound is reacted with oxygen, which produces the maximum amount of CO2?
mcqs.why: The Key Facts state that when one mole of each compound is reacted with oxygen, ethane (C2H6) produces the maximum amount of CO2 among the compounds compared.

mcqs.q: How much 95 percent CaCO3 is required to neutralize 50 cm3 of 0.5 M HCl solution?
mcqs.why: Working: moles of HCl = 0.5 x 50 / 1000 = 0.025 mol; CaCO3 needed = 0.025 / 2 = 0.0125 mol; pure mass = 0.0125 x 100 = 1.25 g; impure mass = 1.25 x 100 / 95 = 1.32 g.

mcqs.q: How many molecules are there in 1.5 g of H2O?
mcqs.why: Working: moles = 1.5 / 18 = 0.0833 mol; molecules = 0.0833 x 6.022 x 10^23 = 5.02 x 10^22 molecules, as shown step by step in the notes.

mcqs.q: How many moles are there in 1.5 g of H2O?
mcqs.why: Working: molar mass of H2O = 18 g/mol; moles = mass / molar mass = 1.5 / 18 = 0.0833 mol, which is step 2 of the calculation in the notes.

mcqs.q: One mole of a substance contains the same number of particles as there are atoms in how much carbon-12?
mcqs.why: The notes define a mole as the amount containing the same number of particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12, and that number is Avogadro number.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the mole from Avogadro number?
options: The mole is a pure number and Avogadro number is a unit
Both the mole and Avogadro number are units
The mole is the unit and Avogadro number is the count of particles in one mole
Avogadro number is a unit of mass in grams

mcqs.q: In balancing Cu + H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + SO2 + H2O, how many molecules of acid are needed to balance the sulphur?

mcqs.q: In the charge-balance method for Ba3N2, what are the total charges of the ions combined?
options: Three Ba2+ give +3 and two N3- give -3
Three Ba2+ give +6 and two N3- give -6
Two Ba2+ give +4 and three N3- give -9
One Ba2+ gives +2 and one N3- gives -3
mcqs.why: Working: 3 x (+2) = +6 from the barium ions and 2 x (-3) = -6 from the nitride ions; the charges cancel exactly, giving the neutral formula Ba3N2.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Notes
lessons.notes_html:
The molecular formula gives the exact number of atoms of each element in one molecule, and two different compounds cannot have exactly the same molecular formula and still be different compounds unless they are isomers, in which case the arrangement differs. The empirical formula gives only the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms, so many different compounds share the same ratio. For example, ethyne C₂H₂ and benzene C₆H₆ both have the empirical formula CH, and glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ and formaldehyde CH₂O both have the empirical formula CH₂O, although their molecules are quite different.

Calcium phosphate: Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ combine as Ca₃(PO₄)₂. Aluminium nitride: Al³⁺ and N³⁻ combine as AlN. Sodium acetate: Na⁺ and CH₃COO⁻ combine as CH₃COONa. Ammonium carbonate: NH₄⁺ and CO₃²⁻ combine as (NH₄)₂CO₃. Bismuth sulphate: Bi³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ combine as Bi₂(SO₄)₃.

mcqs.q: What does the molecular formula of a compound give?
options: Only the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms
The exact number of atoms of each element in one molecule
The total mass of one mole in grams only
The arrangement of atoms but not their numbers
mcqs.why: The notes state that the molecular formula gives the exact number of atoms of each element in one molecule, unlike the empirical formula, which gives only a ratio.

mcqs.q: What does the empirical formula of a compound give?
options: The exact number of atoms in one molecule
The simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms
The molar mass of the compound
The number of molecules in one mole
mcqs.why: The notes state that the empirical formula gives only the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms, so many different compounds can share the same empirical formula.

mcqs.q: Two different compounds can share the same molecular formula only if they are what?
options: Isomers, in which case the arrangement of atoms differs
Elements, in which case the masses differ
mcqs.why: The notes state that two different compounds cannot have exactly the same molecular formula and still be different compounds unless they are isomers, in which case the arrangement differs.

mcqs.q: Ethyne, C2H2, and benzene, C6H6, share which empirical formula?
mcqs.why: Working: C2H2 divided by 2 gives CH, and C6H6 divided by 6 also gives CH, so the notes give CH as the shared empirical formula of ethyne and benzene.

mcqs.q: Glucose, C6H12O6, and formaldehyde, CH2O, share which empirical formula?
mcqs.why: Working: dividing C6H12O6 by 6 gives CH2O, which is itself the molecular formula of formaldehyde, so the notes give CH2O as their shared empirical formula.

mcqs.q: Calcium ions, Ca2+, combine with phosphate ions, PO4 3-, to give which formula?
mcqs.why: Charge balance: 3 x (+2) = +6 and 2 x (-3) = -6, so Ca2+ and PO4 3- combine as Ca3(PO4)2, as given in the notes for calcium phosphate.

mcqs.q: Aluminium ions, Al3+, combine with nitride ions, N3-, to give which formula?
mcqs.why: Charge balance: one Al3+ ion (+3) exactly balances one N3- ion (-3), so aluminium nitride is AlN, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Sodium ions, Na+, combine with acetate ions, CH3COO-, to give which formula?
mcqs.why: Charge balance: one Na+ ion (+1) balances one CH3COO- ion (-1), so sodium acetate is CH3COONa, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Ammonium ions, NH4+, combine with carbonate ions, CO3 2-, to give which formula?
mcqs.why: Charge balance: 2 x (+1) = +2 from two ammonium ions balances one carbonate ion at -2, so ammonium carbonate is (NH4)2CO3, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Bismuth ions, Bi3+, combine with sulphate ions, SO4 2-, to give which formula?
mcqs.why: Charge balance: 2 x (+3) = +6 and 3 x (-2) = -6, so Bi3+ and SO4 2- combine as Bi2(SO4)3, as given in the notes for bismuth sulphate.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
First, the correct chemical formulas of all reactants and products must be known. Second, the equation must be balanced, so that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides, obeying the law of conservation of mass. Third, the physical states of the substances should be shown, and any conditions of the reaction, such as heat, catalyst or pressure, should be written above the arrow.

Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10²³, is the number of particles in one mole of any substance. It is also the number of atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12. The mole is the unit used to count very large numbers of atoms, molecules or ions: one mole of a substance is the amount that contains Avogadro's number of particles, and its mass in grams equals its relative atomic or molecular mass. For example, one mole of water is 18 g and contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.

mcqs.q: Where should reaction conditions such as heat, catalyst or pressure be written in an equation?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the physical states should be shown and any conditions of the reaction, such as heat, catalyst or pressure, should be written above the arrow.

mcqs.q: Avogadro number, 6.022 x 10^23, is also the number of atoms in exactly how much carbon-12?
mcqs.why: The notes state that Avogadro number is the number of particles in one mole of any substance, and it is also the number of atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12.

mcqs.why: The notes give water as the example: one mole of water is 18 g (its relative molecular mass in grams) and contains 6.022 x 10^23 molecules.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • In the reaction H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl carried out in sunlight, the energy to break the bonds of H₂ and Cl₂ comes from sunlight.
  • The reaction NaCl(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq) has the least value of activation energy among the reactions compared in the book.
  • Formation of HI from its elements is an endothermic reaction.
  • A reaction is expected to be reversible when its energy profile shows the products slightly above the reactants.
  • When NaOH and HCl are mixed, the temperature increases: the reaction is exothermic with a negative enthalpy change.
  • The change C (diamond) → C (graphite), with enthalpy change -3 kJ/mol, does not occur readily because it has a high activation energy.

mcqs.q: In the reaction H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl carried out in sunlight, where does the energy to break the bonds of H2 and Cl2 come from?
mcqs.why: The notes state that in this reaction carried out in sunlight, the energy to break the bonds of H2 and Cl2 comes from sunlight.

mcqs.q: Which reaction is stated to have the least value of activation energy among the reactions compared in the book?
options: Formation of HI from its elements
mcqs.why: The notes state that the reaction NaCl(aq) + AgNO3(aq) -> AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq) has the least value of activation energy among those compared.

mcqs.why: The notes explicitly state that formation of HI from its elements is an endothermic reaction, so it takes in heat.

mcqs.q: A reaction is expected to be reversible when its energy profile shows what?
options: Products at exactly the same level as reactants with no barrier
mcqs.why: The notes state a reaction is expected to be reversible when its energy profile shows the products slightly above the reactants.

mcqs.q: When NaOH and HCl are mixed, the temperature increases. What does this show about the reaction?

It is exothermic with a negative enthalpy change
It is reversible with no heat change

mcqs.q: What is the enthalpy change given for C (diamond) -> C (graphite)?
mcqs.why: The notes give the enthalpy change for C (diamond) -> C (graphite) as -3 kJ/mol; the negative sign is checked as -3 < 0.

mcqs.q: Why does C (diamond) -> C (graphite) not occur readily despite its enthalpy change?

mcqs.why: A value of -3 kJ/mol is less than zero, verified as -3 < 0, so the enthalpy change has a negative sign.

mcqs.q: In the H2 + Cl2 reaction in sunlight, which bonds must be broken using the sunlight energy?

mcqs.q: If products lie slightly above reactants on an energy profile, what is expected?

The reaction is expected to be reversible

lessons.title: Worked Notes
lessons.notes_html: A reaction is easily reversible when the energy gap between reactants and products is small, so the reverse reaction also has a small barrier to climb. In graph (b) the products lie only slightly above the reactants, so the reverse barrier is small and the reaction can readily go backwards. In graph (a) the products lie far below the reactants, so the reaction is strongly exothermic and practically goes to completion in the forward direction only.

mcqs.q: A reaction is easily reversible when what condition holds?
options: The energy gap between reactants and products is large
The energy gap between reactants and products is small
The products are far below the reactants
mcqs.why: The notes state a reaction is easily reversible when the energy gap between reactants and products is small.

mcqs.q: Why does a small energy gap make the reverse reaction easier?
options: It makes the forward reaction exothermic only
The reverse reaction also has a small barrier to climb
mcqs.why: With a small gap, the notes explain the reverse reaction also has a small barrier to climb, so it can go backwards readily.

mcqs.q: In graph (b), where do the products lie relative to the reactants?

mcqs.why: The notes describe graph (b) as having products only slightly above the reactants, giving a small reverse barrier.

mcqs.q: In graph (b), what happens because the reverse barrier is small?
options: The reaction can readily go backwards
The reaction goes to completion forward only
mcqs.why: The notes state that in graph (b) the small reverse barrier means the reaction can readily go backwards.

mcqs.q: In graph (a), where do the products lie relative to the reactants?
options: At the same level as reactants
mcqs.why: The notes describe graph (a) as having products far below the reactants, unlike the slight rise in graph (b).

mcqs.q: What type of reaction is described in graph (a) where products lie far below reactants?

lessons.notes_html:
Enthalpy is the total heat content of a system at constant pressure; it is a property of the substances themselves. Enthalpy change is the difference between the enthalpies of the products and the reactants, that is, the heat absorbed or given out by a reaction at constant pressure. Atoms in a bond are held together by attractive forces, and energy must be supplied to pull them apart against that attraction. Since energy is taken in from the surroundings to break the bond, bond breaking is always an endothermic process. Bond formation, on the other hand, releases energy and is exothermic.

Draw two energy profiles on the same axes, both starting at the same reactant level and ending at the same lower product level, because both reactions are exothermic. The faster reaction has a lower peak, that is, a smaller activation energy, so more molecules can cross its barrier at a given temperature. The slower reaction has a higher peak, a larger activation energy, so fewer molecules can cross it and the reaction moves more slowly.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Heat is energy in transit: it is the energy transferred from one body to another because of a difference in temperature, and it is not stored in a body. Enthalpy is a property of a system: it is the total heat content of the system at constant pressure. When a reaction takes place at constant pressure, the heat absorbed or given out by the system equals its change in enthalpy, but heat itself is only the energy that flows during the change.

An exothermic reaction gives out heat to the surroundings, so the temperature rises and delta H is negative. Examples are the combustion of methane or petrol, the neutralisation of an acid with a base, and respiration in living cells. An endothermic reaction takes in heat from the surroundings, so the temperature falls and delta H is positive. Examples are photosynthesis in plants, the melting of ice, the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate into lime and carbon dioxide, and the dissolving of ammonium chloride in water.

A reaction takes place when reactant particles collide with one another. Only collisions with enough energy, at least equal to the activation energy, and with the correct orientation are effective. In an effective collision the old bonds break and new bonds form through an unstable arrangement called the transition state or activated complex, which sits at the top of the energy barrier. The activated complex then breaks down into the products, and the net energy difference between reactants and products appears as heat absorbed or given out.

Activation energy is the minimum extra energy that reactant molecules must gain before they can react; it is the height of the energy barrier between reactants and products. The transition state is the unstable, highest-energy arrangement of atoms at the top of that barrier, in which old bonds are partly broken and new bonds are partly formed. The system is the part of the universe under study, for example the reacting mixture in a beaker. The surroundings are everything else around the system that can exchange energy with it.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Facts to Remember

  • If the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are very high, the equilibrium point is reached very soon.
  • In the presence of lightning, N₂ and O₂ of the atmosphere react with each other.
  • Lime (CaO) is produced in maximum amount by heating limestone, CaCO₃, at high temperature in an open vessel.
  • A reversible reaction achieves the state of equilibrium when the concentrations of all the reactants and the products become constant.

  • For the reaction CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) in a closed vessel, increasing the pressure favours the backward reaction.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
In dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions both continue to take place, but at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant although the reactions never stop. In static equilibrium nothing at all happens: no reaction takes place in either direction, as in a book resting on a table, where the forces balance but there is no movement or change.

The decomposition of water into hydrogen and oxygen is an endothermic reaction, because energy must be supplied to split water. Increasing the temperature therefore favours the forward reaction, and more water decomposes to give more hydrogen and oxygen, shifting the equilibrium to the right.

Maximum yield is obtained by shifting the equilibrium as far as possible towards the products, following Le Chatelier's principle: add more reactants, remove a product as soon as it forms, choose the temperature that favours the forward reaction, and, where the number of gas molecules changes, choose the pressure that favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Using a catalyst does not change the yield; it only helps equilibrium to be reached faster.

Equilibrium is reached faster by increasing the rates of both the forward and the reverse reactions. This is done by adding a catalyst, by raising the temperature, and by increasing the concentrations of the reactants or the pressure of the gases. The position of equilibrium itself is not changed by a catalyst; only the time needed to reach it becomes shorter.

There is no effect. The left side has two moles of gas (one of nitrogen plus one of oxygen) and the right side also has two moles of gas (two of nitric oxide). Since the number of gas molecules is the same on both sides, changing the pressure does not shift the equilibrium in either direction.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Notes
lessons.notes_html:
A reaction is irreversible when its products cannot easily react back to give the reactants, usually because a product escapes from the mixture as a gas, separates as an insoluble precipitate, or because the reaction releases so much energy that the reverse barrier is too high. A reaction is reversible when it takes place in a closed system, its products remain in contact with each other, and the energy barrier for the reverse reaction is small enough for the products to react back.

Combustion reactions are generally irreversible because their products, carbon dioxide and water vapour, escape into the air together with a large amount of heat and light. The products are no longer held together in a closed system, and they cannot recombine on their own to form the fuel again. The reaction therefore goes practically to completion in the forward direction.

A reaction is reversible if, in a closed vessel, it does not go to completion but reaches a state where reactants and products are both present in constant amounts, and if changing the conditions, such as temperature, pressure or concentration, shifts the mixture back or forward. A reaction is irreversible if it goes to completion, if a product escapes or precipitates out, and if the original reactants cannot be recovered from the products by changing the conditions.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
(a) To drive the reaction forward: add more reactant, remove a product as it forms, raise the temperature if the forward reaction is endothermic (or lower it if the forward reaction is exothermic), and raise the pressure if the forward side has fewer gas molecules.
(b) To drive it backward: do the opposite, that is, add more product, remove a reactant, change the temperature in the opposite direction, or change the pressure to favour the side with more gas molecules.

At the start only reactants are present, so the forward reaction is fast and the reverse reaction cannot take place at all. As reactants are used up and products build up, the forward rate falls because the reactant concentration falls, while the reverse rate rises because the product concentration rises. The two rates keep approaching each other until they become equal. At that point equilibrium is reached, and both reactions continue at the same rate, so no further change in concentration is seen.

A catalyst speeds up both the forward and the reverse reactions by the same factor, because it lowers the activation energy of both directions equally. Equilibrium is therefore reached much faster, but the position of equilibrium and the final amounts of reactants and products remain exactly the same as they would be without the catalyst.

A reversible reaction can be forced to completion by continuously removing one of its products from the mixture, so that the reverse reaction has nothing to react back with and the forward reaction keeps going. This is done by letting a gaseous product escape, by precipitating a product as an insoluble solid, or by using a large excess of one reactant. In each case Le Chatelier's principle keeps pulling the equilibrium forward until the other reactant is used up.

Increasing the temperature favours the endothermic direction of a reversible reaction, and decreasing the temperature favours the exothermic direction. For example, in an exothermic forward reaction, heating shifts the equilibrium backwards towards the reactants, while cooling shifts it forwards towards the products. Temperature is the only factor that changes the value of the equilibrium constant itself; concentration, pressure and catalysts only shift the position or the speed.

options: Add more reactant and remove a product as it forms
Change temperature opposite to forward favour
mcqs.why: To drive forward: add more reactant, remove a product as it forms, choose temperature favouring forward, and pressure favouring fewer gas molecules.

mcqs.q: To drive a reaction backward, what should be done?
options: Do the opposite: add more product, remove a reactant, change temperature and pressure oppositely
Add a catalyst to shift position
mcqs.why: Driving backward is the opposite: add product, remove reactant, and change temperature or pressure in the opposite direction.

mcqs.why: At the start only reactants are present, so forward reaction is fast and reverse cannot take place at all, as described.

mcqs.q: As reactants are used up and products build up, what happens to the rates?

mcqs.why: Forward rate falls as reactant concentration falls, reverse rate rises as product concentration rises, until they become equal at equilibrium.

mcqs.why: At equilibrium both reactions continue at the same rate, so no further change in concentration is seen.

Calcium reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to form calcium sulphate and hydrogen gas: Ca + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂. The reaction starts vigorously but soon slows down, because the calcium sulphate formed is only sparingly soluble and coats the metal, partly stopping further attack by the acid.

A Bronsted-Lowry acid is a substance that donates a proton (H+) to another substance. The hydrogen sulphate ion donates a proton to water or to a base, forming the sulphate ion: HSO₄⁻ → SO₄²⁻ + H⁺. The hydrochloric acid in the stomach is very dilute, about 0.1 M, and the stomach wall is protected by a thick layer of mucus that stops the acid from attacking the tissue. lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
According to Arrhenius, an acid is a substance that releases hydrogen ions (H+) when dissolved in water, for example HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻, and H₂SO₄ → 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻. A base is a substance that releases hydroxide ions (OH-) in water, for example NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻. An acid and a base neutralise each other to form a salt and water, because the H⁺ and OH⁻ ions combine to form water. The concept is limited because it applies only to water solutions and cannot explain substances like ammonia, which acts as a base without containing OH⁻.

Arrhenius defines an acid as a producer of H⁺ ions in water and a base as a producer of OH⁻ ions in water, so it works only in water solution. Bronsted-Lowry defines an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor, in any solvent and even without water. Every Arrhenius acid is also a Bronsted-Lowry acid, but the Bronsted-Lowry concept is wider: it covers ammonia as a base, since NH₃ accepts a proton to become NH₄⁺, and it explains conjugate acid-base pairs, such as CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻.

With ammonium chloride: H₂SO₄ + NH₄Cl → NH₄HSO₄ + HCl, and hydrogen chloride gas is released. With ammonium nitrate: H₂SO₄ + NH₄NO₃ → NH₄HSO₄ + HNO₃, and nitric acid is released. With magnesium oxide: H₂SO₄ + MgO → MgSO₄ + H₂O, a neutralisation reaction giving magnesium sulphate. With magnesium carbonate: H₂SO₄ + MgCO₃ → MgSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂, giving magnesium sulphate with the release of carbon dioxide gas.

When a base reacts with a non-metallic oxide, a salt and water are formed, just as in neutralisation. For example, 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O, and Ca(OH)₂ + SO₂ → CaSO₃ + H₂O. Since the non-metallic oxide behaves like an acid towards a base, we infer that non-metallic oxides are acidic in nature. They are therefore called acidic oxides, and they form acids when dissolved in water.

Dry hydrogen chloride gas shows no acidic character by itself, because acidity needs free hydrogen ions, and dry HCl molecules do not release H⁺ ions. It does not turn dry blue litmus paper red. When HCl is dissolved in water, its molecules ionise completely to give H⁺ (as H3O+) and Cl⁻ ions, and these hydrogen ions give the solution its acidic character: it turns blue litmus red and reacts with bases and metals. In short, the gas is not acidic, but its water solution is strongly acidic.

An acid and its conjugate base differ by exactly one proton. The acid is the species that donates the proton, and the conjugate base is what remains after the proton has been donated. For example, in the pair CH₃COOH / CH₃COO⁻, acetic acid is the acid and the acetate ion is its conjugate base. A strong acid has a weak conjugate base, and a weak acid has a comparatively strong conjugate base, because the two members of the pair are linked by the gain or loss of one H⁺ ion.

lessons.notes_html:
Atomic number was chosen because the properties of elements repeat periodically with atomic number, as Moseley showed. Arranging by atomic mass caused problems: argon (mass 40) would come after potassium (mass 39) although argon belongs before it, and cobalt and nickel, tellurium and iodine showed similar inversions. Atomic number removed all these anomalies and gave every element its correct place.

Periodic means repeating at regular intervals. In the periodic table, elements with similar properties recur at regular intervals when they are arranged in order of atomic number, because their outer electronic configurations repeat. This repetition of properties is called periodicity.

Each period fills a new set of sub-shells, and the higher periods have more sub-shells available to fill. The first period fills only the 1s sub-shell and holds 2 elements, the second and third periods fill s and p sub-shells and hold 8 each, the fourth and fifth also fill d sub-shells and hold 18 each, and the sixth also fills f sub-shells and holds 32. Periods therefore grow longer as we move down the table.

Elements are placed in a group according to their outer electronic configuration. When atomic number increases down a group, each new element adds a whole new shell, but the number of electrons in the outermost shell stays the same, because the group number itself is fixed by that outer-shell count. Hence all elements of one group have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties.

In the third period, sodium (Na) has the maximum atomic radius and chlorine (Cl) has the minimum atomic radius, argon being a noble gas left out of the comparison. Across a period the nuclear charge increases and pulls the electron shells inward, so the radius decreases from left to right.

The first ionisation energy removes an electron from a neutral magnesium atom, Mg, to give Mg⁺. The second ionisation energy removes an electron from Mg⁺, which already carries a positive charge and holds its remaining electrons more tightly, and which has the stable configuration 2,8. More energy is therefore needed to remove the second electron than the first.

The least ionisation energy belongs to the alkali metals at the bottom left of the table, caesium (and francium), because their single outer electron is far from the nucleus and well shielded, so it is lost very easily. The highest electronegativity belongs to fluorine, at the top right of the table, because its small atom attracts a shared pair of electrons more strongly than any other element.

The new element would be placed by its atomic number, in the position following the element before it, because atomic number fixes the order of the table. Its group would be fixed by the number of electrons in its outermost shell, and its period by the number of shells its electrons occupy. If its electronic configuration were known, its exact block and neighbours would follow at once.

The first element of the periodic table is hydrogen, with atomic number 1 and one electron in its first shell. Hydrogen can do either: it can lose its electron to form the positive hydrogen ion H⁺, as in acids, or it can gain one electron to complete its shell and form the negative hydride ion H⁻, as in sodium hydride. Its behaviour depends on the element it reacts with.

Nitrogen has five electrons in its outer shell, so accepting three more completes its octet of eight, giving N³⁻. Oxygen already has six outer electrons and needs only two more to complete its octet, giving O²⁻. Accepting a third electron would give oxygen ten electrons around it, more than an octet, and the second shell has no d orbitals to hold extra electrons. Moreover, adding a third negative charge to an already doubly negative ion is opposed by strong repulsion. O³⁻ therefore cannot form.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
To locate an element without its atomic number, we need its electronic configuration, especially the number of shells and the number of outer-shell electrons, together with its chemical properties, such as its valency and the kind of compounds it forms. Atomic mass is not reliable for this purpose: isotopes of one element have different masses, and the mass order itself misplaces some elements, as with argon and potassium and with cobalt and nickel.

There are four blocks in the periodic table: the s-block, the p-block, the d-block and the f-block, named after the sub-shell into which the last electron enters. Yes, the blocks are very helpful: the s-block holds reactive metals, the p-block holds most non-metals and metalloids, the d-block holds the transition metals, and the f-block holds the inner transition metals. Knowing the block at once suggests the valency, metallic character and typical compounds of an element.

(a) Atomic radius decreases across a period from left to right. The electrons are added to the same shell, while the nuclear charge increases, so the nucleus pulls the whole shell inward more strongly.
(b) Ionisation energy increases across a period. The same increasing nuclear pull holds the outer electrons more tightly, and the decreasing size brings them closer to the nucleus, so more energy is needed to remove an electron.

Melting and boiling points, electrical conductivity, hardness, density and solubility give strong clues. A high melting point with conduction when molten points to ionic bonding; a low melting point with no conduction points to covalent molecules; a high melting point with conduction in the solid state and the ability to be beaten into sheets points to metallic bonding. Lustre and malleability further confirm the metallic character.

Four non-metals that are solids at normal temperature are carbon, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine. Others are boron, silicon and selenium. Most non-metals are gases at room temperature, but these have strong bonds or strong forces between their particles that keep them solid.

As we move down group 1 the atoms become larger, because a new shell is added at each step, and the metallic bond between them becomes weaker. The metal therefore becomes softer and easier to cut: lithium is fairly hard, sodium cuts easily, and potassium and caesium are softer still.

Potassium will react very vigorously with halogens, even more violently than sodium. It loses its single outer electron very easily, and the halogen gains it readily, so the reaction is fast and strongly exothermic. With chlorine, for example, potassium burns with a lilac flame to form potassium chloride, KCl.

The reducing agent is sodium bromide, that is, the bromide ion Br⁻. Chlorine is reduced as it gains electrons to become chloride ions, while the bromide ions lose electrons and are oxidised to bromine. The substance that is itself oxidised is the reducing agent, so NaBr is the reducing agent.

Iodine molecules are large and contain many electrons, so the London dispersion forces between them are strong. A large amount of heat energy is needed to separate the molecules, so iodine remains a solid at room temperature, whereas the smaller halogens chlorine and fluorine, with much weaker forces, are gases.

Helium should have the lowest boiling point of all the noble gases. Helium atoms are the smallest and contain only two electrons, so the forces between them are the weakest of all. Almost no energy is needed to separate helium atoms, so helium boils at -269 C, lower than any other element.

Metals are solids because the strong metallic bond holds their atoms firmly in a regular lattice, and a large amount of energy is needed to break that lattice. Non-metals form small covalent molecules held together only by weak intermolecular forces, so many of them are gases at room temperature. Those non-metals that form giant covalent structures, like carbon and sulphur, or large molecules, like iodine, are solids.

Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine. Chlorine atoms are smaller and more electronegative, so they attract and gain electrons more readily than bromine atoms. This is shown directly by the displacement reaction: chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide, giving sodium chloride and bromine, while bromine cannot displace chlorine from sodium chloride.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
A catalytic converter is fitted in the exhaust system of a car to clean up the exhaust gases before they reach the air. Its catalyst, usually platinum, palladium and rhodium, converts poisonous carbon monoxide into harmless carbon dioxide, converts unburnt hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water, and converts harmful nitrogen oxides into harmless nitrogen gas. The catalyst itself is not used up, and the converter greatly reduces air pollution from vehicles.

Alkali metals react by losing their outer electron. Down the group the atoms get larger, the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded, so it is lost more easily and reactivity increases. Halogens react by gaining an electron. Down the group the atoms get larger, the incoming electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is gained less easily and reactivity decreases. The two groups therefore show opposite trends.

Metals are tough and strong because the metallic bond holds their ions in a regular lattice with a sea of mobile electrons: when a force is applied, layers slip but the bond holds, so the metal bends instead of breaking. Non-metals have no such bond: their molecules are held only by weak intermolecular forces, or their crystals are brittle, so they break or crumble under a force instead of bending. They are therefore neither tough nor strong.

Alkali metals and halogens are both very reactive, but in opposite ways. Alkali metals have one electron in their outer shell, which they lose very easily, so they act as strong reducing agents and form positive ions. Halogens have seven electrons in their outer shell and need only one more to complete it, so they gain electrons very easily, acting as strong oxidising agents and forming negative ions. One group gives electrons, the other takes them, and together they form stable ionic compounds such as sodium chloride.

Metals are usually lustrous solids with high melting and boiling points, except mercury, which is a liquid. They are good conductors of heat and electricity, and they can be beaten into sheets and drawn into wires. Non-metals may be solids, liquids or gases at room temperature and show a wide range of melting and boiling points. They are poor conductors of heat and electricity, except graphite, they are brittle, and they are dull and cannot be polished, except iodine. Metals are generally tough and strong; non-metals are neither tough nor strong.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
The main objective of environmental education is to make people aware of the environment and its problems, and to give them the knowledge, attitudes and skills needed to protect it. An environmentally educated person understands how human actions affect air, water, soil and living things, and takes part in solving environmental problems.

Particulate matter is released by the burning of fuels in vehicles, factories and power stations, by industrial processes such as crushing and grinding, by construction work, by the burning of crop residue and wood, and by natural sources such as dust storms, forest fires and volcanic eruptions. These tiny solid and liquid particles stay suspended in the air and are breathed into the lungs.

Carbon monoxide, CO, is far more poisonous than carbon dioxide. Carbon monoxide combines with the haemoglobin in red blood cells about 200 to 300 times more strongly than oxygen does, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, so the blood can no longer carry enough oxygen to the body, and a person can suffocate. Carbon dioxide is harmful mainly in large amounts, because it displaces oxygen and causes suffocation, but it does not poison the blood in this way.

Acid rain damages the leaves of trees directly, so they cannot photosynthesise properly. It also washes important nutrients such as calcium and magnesium out of the soil, and it releases harmful aluminium from the soil, which damages the roots. Trees therefore grow weakly, become open to disease, and large areas of forest can die.

When fossil fuels containing sulphur are burnt, the sulphur burns to form sulphur dioxide gas. Sulphur dioxide irritates the eyes, nose and lungs and causes breathing diseases, and in the air it is oxidised and dissolved in rain water to form sulphuric acid, which falls as acid rain. Acid rain damages crops, forests, buildings and water life.

Wind energy is a clean and renewable source of energy that does not burn fuel and does not pollute the air. Windmills and wind turbines turn the energy of moving air into electricity for homes and industry, into mechanical work for pumping water and grinding grain, and into power for remote areas. It costs no fuel once built and helps to reduce the use of fossil fuels.

Insecticides and pesticides sprayed on crops enter the food chain: insects eat the poison, and birds eat the poisoned insects, so the poison builds up in the birds' bodies. Some pesticides, such as DDT, thin the shells of birds' eggs, so the eggs break before the chicks hatch. Pesticides also kill the insects that many birds feed on, so birds starve, and the poisoned birds themselves may die.

Even at only 0.04 percent, carbon dioxide is the most important greenhouse gas produced by human activity, because it absorbs the infrared radiation given off by the Earth and traps heat in the atmosphere. It also stays in the air for hundreds of years, so every extra bit adds to the total. A small rise in its percentage therefore warms the whole planet, disturbs rainfall, melts ice and threatens the balance of the ecosystem.

Only gases that can absorb infrared radiation cause the greenhouse effect. Carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour and ozone have molecular structures that vibrate when they absorb infrared rays, so they trap heat. The main gases of the air, nitrogen and oxygen, are simple two-atom molecules that do not absorb infrared radiation, so they let the heat pass through and cause no greenhouse effect, even though they are present in far larger amounts.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Carbon monoxide is poisonous because it stops the blood from carrying oxygen. Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides irritate the eyes and lungs, cause asthma and bronchitis, and form acid rain. Particulate matter lodges in the lungs and causes breathing and heart diseases. Ground-level ozone damages the lungs and crops. Lead damages the brain and nervous system, especially in children. Together these pollutants reduce visibility as smog and damage buildings, crops and water life.

The greenhouse effect is the warming of the Earth by gases in the atmosphere that let the Sun's short-wave radiation in but absorb the long-wave infrared radiation given off by the Earth, trapping heat like the glass of a greenhouse. Global warming is dangerous because it melts glaciers and polar ice, raising sea levels and flooding coastal areas; it disturbs rainfall, causing droughts in some places and floods in others; it increases heatwaves, storms and diseases; and it destroys habitats, crops and water supplies on which life depends.

The air quality index is a number scale used to report how clean or polluted the air is at a place, and what health effects the pollution may cause. A low value means the air is good and healthy, while a high value means the air is unhealthy, especially for sensitive people. It conveys, in one simple number and colour, the levels of pollutants such as particulate matter, ozone, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide, and it tells people whether it is safe to go outdoors.

High risk groups are children, elderly people, pregnant women, and people already suffering from asthma, heart disease or other lung diseases. Pollution is more dangerous for them because children's lungs and immune systems are still developing, elderly people's defences are weaker, and people with existing diseases have little reserve to fight further damage. Even pollution levels that healthy adults can tolerate can cause serious illness in these groups.

First, reduce pollution at its source: use cleaner fuels, fit filters and catalytic converters, treat industrial waste, and shift to renewable energy such as solar and wind power. Second, protect and restore nature: plant trees, save forests, conserve water, and recycle waste instead of dumping it. Third, make and enforce laws and spread awareness: governments set emission limits, schools teach environmental education, and people use public transport, save energy and avoid single-use plastics.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Organic compounds contain carbon, usually combined with hydrogen, and are generally covalent, with low melting and boiling points, they are often flammable, and their reactions are slow. Inorganic compounds are generally the compounds of metals and non-metals, salts, acids and bases, often ionic, with high melting and boiling points, and their reactions are usually fast. Carbonates, cyanides and oxides of carbon are exceptions and are classed as inorganic.

Organic compounds are so numerous because of carbon's unique properties. Carbon forms strong bonds with itself, called catenation, giving long chains, branched chains and rings. Carbon is tetravalent and forms single, double and triple bonds with carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and halogens. The same set of atoms can also be arranged in different ways, giving isomers. Together these properties produce millions of different compounds.

When natural gas, which is mainly methane, is oxidised under controlled conditions with a limited supply of oxygen, methanol (CH₃OH) is obtained. On further controlled oxidation, methanol gives formaldehyde (HCHO), and then formic acid. Complete oxidation, by contrast, gives only carbon dioxide and water.

Naphtha is decomposed by cracking: it is heated to about 500 C in the presence of a catalyst called zeolite. The large hydrocarbon molecules break apart into smaller, more useful molecules, giving a mixture of alkanes and alkenes containing five to ten carbon atoms. Cracking thus turns the less wanted heavy fractions into petrol-range fuels and chemical feedstocks.

Molecular formula: C₄H₁₀. Structural formula: a central CH group joined to three CH₃ groups, written as CH₃-CH(CH₃)-CH₃, with the middle carbon bonded to one hydrogen, two CH₃ groups in the chain and one CH₃ branch. Condensed structural formula: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃.

Organic compounds are useful in almost every part of life. They give us fuels such as petrol, diesel and natural gas; food such as carbohydrates, proteins, fats and vitamins; medicines and drugs; clothes made of cotton, wool and synthetic fibres; plastics, paints, dyes, soaps and detergents; and the paper, rubber and explosives used in industry. Life itself is built of organic compounds.

Five organic compounds found in nature are methane, from natural gas and marshes; glucose, made by plants in photosynthesis; cellulose, the material of plant cell walls and cotton; starch, stored in potatoes, rice and wheat; and proteins, which build the bodies of animals and plants.

Step 1: Find the longest continuous chain: it has four carbon atoms, so the parent is butane.
Step 2: Number the chain from the end nearer the branch: the branch falls on carbon 2.
Step 3: The branch is a methyl group. The IUPAC name is therefore 2-methylbutane.

Melting and boiling points increase as we move from lower to higher members of the alkane series. Larger molecules have more electrons and stronger London dispersion forces between them, so more heat energy is needed to separate them. Methane and ethane are gases, the middle members are liquids, and the higher members are waxy solids.

lessons.notes_html:
Alkanes show little reactivity because their C-C and C-H bonds are strong, almost non-polar and fully shared, since the electronegativity values of carbon (2.6) and hydrogen (2.1) differ very little. There is no polar site and no free electron pair for acids, bases or oxidising agents to attack. Alkanes are therefore called paraffins, meaning little affinity, and they react only under vigorous conditions, as in combustion and chlorination.

Natural gas is mainly methane, which burns in air to give carbon dioxide and water with the release of a large amount of heat. When methane is mixed with air in the right proportion and then ignited, every part of the mixture burns at once, and the sudden release of heat expands the gases violently. This rapid combustion is an explosion, and it is the main cause of explosions in homes where gas has leaked and mixed with air.

Inorganic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points, because they are often ionic or giant structures held together by strong electrostatic or metallic forces, and a large amount of energy is needed to break them. Organic compounds generally have low melting and boiling points, because they are covalent molecules held together only by weak intermolecular forces, which are easily overcome by heat. Inorganic salts like sodium chloride melt near 800 C, while organic liquids like petrol boil well below 200 C.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Organic compounds run daily life. Food, the carbohydrates, proteins, fats and vitamins we eat, are organic compounds. Clothes of cotton, wool, silk and synthetic fibres are organic. Medicines, soaps, detergents, cosmetics, paints and dyes are organic. Fuels for cooking, transport and power stations are organic hydrocarbons. Plastics, rubber, paper and furniture materials are organic compounds. Without organic chemistry there would be no food, fuel, medicine or modern industry.

Carbon is important because it alone combines four properties no other element shares to the same degree. It forms four strong covalent bonds, it bonds to itself in long chains, branches and rings (catenation), it forms single, double and triple bonds, and it bonds with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur and halogens. These properties produce millions of compounds, including every compound of life, so a whole branch of chemistry, organic chemistry, is devoted to carbon compounds.

A functional group is the part of a molecule that fixes its chemical behaviour, that is, the site where reactions take place. The C-C single bond in alkanes is strong, non-polar and fully shared, so no reagent can attack it, and it does not direct the reactions of the molecule. The C=C double bond in alkenes contains a pi bond, whose electrons are exposed and loosely held, so reagents attack it readily and addition reactions take place there. The double bond therefore behaves as a functional group, while the single bond does not.

In the IUPAC system for alkanes, first find the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms; its length gives the parent name, using meth- for one, eth- for two, prop- for three, but- for four, pent- for five, and so on, with the suffix -ane. Second, number the chain from the end nearer a branch, so that branches get the lowest possible numbers. Third, name each branch as an alkyl group, such as methyl or ethyl, and write its position number before its name. If two or more identical branches occur, use di-, tri- or tetra-, for example 2,2-dimethylbutane for a butane chain with two methyl groups on carbon 2.

The combustion of alkanes is useful because it releases a large amount of heat energy. We burn natural gas and LPG for cooking and heating, petrol and diesel in engines for transport, kerosene in lamps and stoves, and coal, oil and gas in power stations to make electricity. Combustion also provides heat for industry, for example in furnaces and kilns. In every case the useful product is the heat energy released when carbon dioxide and water are formed.

  • In case of a fire drill in the laboratory, close gas valves and turn off all equipment.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Common corrosive chemicals are concentrated sulphuric acid, concentrated nitric acid, concentrated hydrochloric acid, sodium hydroxide (caustic soda), potassium hydroxide (caustic potash), and strong bleaching solutions. All of them destroy skin and other living tissue on contact and damage eyes, clothes and bench surfaces.

Explosive chemicals are stored in small amounts in cool, dry places away from flames, heat, shocks and friction. They are never heated directly, never shaken or dropped, and are handled gently with protective equipment. Containers are kept tightly closed and labelled, and only the small amount needed is taken to the bench at a time.

Signs and symbols are posted to warn everyone at a glance about the dangers inside a laboratory or a bottle, even before reading any text. They show whether a substance is corrosive, flammable, toxic or explosive, and they guide safe handling, storage and first aid. Clear labelling prevents mistakes, such as using the wrong chemical, and helps people act correctly in an emergency.

A chemical fire should be handled by first raising the alarm and switching off gas and electricity if it is safe to do so. The right extinguisher must be used: a carbon dioxide or dry powder extinguisher for most chemical and electrical fires, never water on burning oil, solvents or live equipment. If the fire is large, everyone must evacuate at once and the fire service must be called; no one should risk their life to save equipment.

Emergency drills are important because they train students and staff to act quickly and correctly instead of panicking when a real emergency happens. In drills people practise evacuating, using extinguishers, closing gas valves and helping the injured, and the equipment is checked to see that it works. A practised team saves lives and property that an untrained group would lose.

lessons.title: Constructed Response Notes
lessons.notes_html:
First, stay calm and raise the alarm so that everyone evacuates. Switch off the main power supply if it can be done safely, because water or foam on a live electrical fire is deadly. Use a carbon dioxide or dry powder extinguisher on the fire, never water. Close doors to confine the fire, keep away from smoke, and call the fire service and assist the emergency staff when they arrive.

Reactions that release toxic, irritating or foul-smelling gases and vapours must be carried out in a fume cupboard. Examples are reactions giving off chlorine, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, ammonia or hydrogen chloride gas, reactions with volatile acids, and any work with toxic or strongly smelling chemicals. The fume cupboard draws the harmful vapours away from the worker and out of the laboratory.

Some chemicals, such as explosives and certain peroxides, are unstable and need only a small amount of activation energy to start breaking down. A sudden shock, a knock, friction or a sharp blow supplies that energy all at once, and the decomposition then releases a large amount of heat and gas in a fraction of a second. The rapid release of gas and heat is the explosion, which is why such chemicals must never be shaken, dropped or struck.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Explosive chemicals can detonate on heating, shock or friction, causing fire, blast, flying glass and serious injuries, and they can destroy the laboratory. Toxic chemicals poison the body when breathed in, swallowed or absorbed through the skin: they can damage the lungs, liver, kidneys and nervous system, and some cause cancer or unconsciousness. Both kinds of chemicals must be stored safely, used in small amounts, and handled only with protective equipment and proper ventilation.

First, always wear safety goggles, a lab coat and gloves, and tie back long hair. Second, never taste a chemical and never smell it directly; waft the vapour gently towards the nose if the teacher asks. Third, always add acid to water slowly, never water to acid, when diluting. Fourth, read the label of every bottle before use, and never use an unlabelled chemical. Fifth, know the emergency exits, the position of the fire extinguisher, the safety shower and the first aid box, and report every accident to the teacher at once.

Warning signs and symbols are important because they give instant information about danger without needing words or a long explanation. A student who sees a flame symbol knows the substance is flammable, a skull warns of poison, and a corrosive symbol warns that contact destroys skin. This instant warning stops careless handling, reminds workers of the right precautions, and in an emergency it helps rescuers know at once what kind of danger they face, so accidents are prevented before they happen.

Some toxic chemicals are chlorine, ammonia, hydrogen sulphide, carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, mercury and cyanide compounds. If a toxic gas spreads in the laboratory, it is breathed into the lungs and can cause coughing, choking, headache, dizziness and unconsciousness, and in high amounts it can kill. Eyes and skin are also irritated. Everyone must leave the room at once, doors should be closed to confine the gas, ventilation and the fume system should be used, and the teacher and emergency staff must be informed immediately.

First, stay calm, raise the alarm and evacuate everyone from the area, keeping all flames, sparks and electrical equipment away because the chemical is explosive. Remove the student's contaminated clothes at once and wash the affected skin with plenty of running water for at least fifteen minutes. Do not rub the skin and do not try to neutralise the chemical on the body. Call the teacher and the emergency staff, keep the student under observation, and let trained staff clean the spill with the correct absorbent and protective equipment.
